extracted.intended_audience: agency rulemaking staff, administrative law scholars, and policymakers concerned with public comment integrity
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and evaluative criteria for how agencies should detect, treat, and respond to mass, computer-generated, and malattributed public comments in notice-and-comment rulemaking, balancing legal obligations under the APA with practical and technological approaches.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reasoned decisionmaking when relying on malattributed comments
rubrics_metrics.description: An agency's reliance on a comment submitted under a false name is governed by the APA requirement of reasoned decisionmaking (5 U.S.C. § 706(2)(a)); there is no per se rule forbidding or requiring reliance on malattributed comments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: It would be arbitrary and capricious to rely on malattributed comments as a measure of public sentiment or to rely on a comment that purports to be from an authority when it was not. Conversely, if a malattributed comment is relevant, factually accurate, and communicates something of value, the agency may lawfully use it. Treatment is case-specific; agencies should evaluate whether reliance on such comments meets reasoned-decisionmaking standards (examples: avoid treating a malattributed 'expert' comment as authoritative; permit use of accurate substantive content regardless of name).

rubrics_metrics.name: Substance over identity: relevance, factual accuracy, and communicative value
rubrics_metrics.description: Comments should be assessed primarily on whether they are relevant to the rulemaking, factually accurate, and provide useful information, irrespective of the name under which they were submitted.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the content is relevant and accurate, the agency may consider it even if malattributed. The agency 'will take the comment for what it is worth; the name adds nothing to its weight' when the identity is unknown or unremarkable. Agencies should prioritize substantive issues raised over submitter identity except where provenance affects weight.

rubrics_metrics.name: Weight of a comment depends on claimed identity or credentials
rubrics_metrics.description: When a comment claims particular experience, situated knowledge, or expert credentials, the identity and provenance may materially affect how much weight the agency should give the comment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a commenter asserts specialized experience (researcher, regulated party, person directly affected), agencies should prefer signed, verifiable submissions and may seek to verify provenance before affording extra weight. Malattribution that masks biographical misrepresentation increases the risk of inappropriate reliance. Agencies may use internet searches or other verification steps when such claims materially affect deliberations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid being misled about public sentiment by mass or malattributed submissions
rubrics_metrics.description: Agencies should not treat large numbers of identical or near-identical comments as equivalent to independent expressions of public sentiment without assessing whether they reflect orchestrated or automated campaigns.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider whether 100,000 identical comments represent 100,000 individuals or echoes of a single campaign. Malattribution (attaching different names/emails) can make automated, single-source campaigns appear as broad support. Agencies should factor in duplication, timing patterns, and other forensic indicators when interpreting apparent volume as public opinion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider harms to individuals whose identities are used
rubrics_metrics.description: Malattributed comments can cause psychological distress and reputational harm to persons whose names and email addresses are used without permission, even if not rising to statutory identity-theft.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Agencies should recognize potential victim harms (annoyance, anger, reputational damage if a comment goes viral) and consider remedies such as removing fraudulent filings, notifying affected individuals where appropriate, and coordinating with authorities. Quantification of harm is difficult and assessments will vary by case.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of user notices and legal deterrents to discourage malattribution
rubrics_metrics.description: Prominently display terms of participation and warning language that false statements about identity may violate federal law (e.g., 18 U.S.C. § 1028 and other statutes) as part of a deterrence strategy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Regulations.gov's user notice, which warns that knowingly making materially false statements about identity may be a federal crime and that by submitting users verify they are not making such statements, is an example. Such notices may deter individuals but are unlikely to deter large-scale automated operations; visibility and placement of the notice matter.

rubrics_metrics.name: Establish protocols for identifying and handling malattributed comments
rubrics_metrics.description: Agencies should develop policies and procedures to determine whether a comment is malattributed and how to handle it in the docket.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Policies should address whether agencies will (a) attempt to resolve provenance, (b) flag potential malattributions, (c) remove fraudulent comments, and (d) allocate staff to assist investigations or prosecutions when criminal conduct is suspected. Many agencies lack such protocols; creating them clarifies responsibilities and responses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider authentication technologies, balancing verification and anonymity
rubrics_metrics.description: A range of authentication technologies (secure login, two-factor authentication, biometrics, security questions, database verification, extra consent clicks) exist to verify submitters, but implementing them is in tension with policies permitting anonymous comments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Agencies must weigh technical feasibility and privacy/anonymity policies. Some authentication (e.g., identity verification for certain submitters) may be appropriate, but wholesale identity verification conflicts with norms and legal allowances for anonymous participation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Implement bot-detection and 'speed-bump' tools (CAPTCHA/reCAPTCHA)
rubrics_metrics.description: Use human-verification tools (CAPTCHA, reCAPTCHA) and other speed bumps to reduce automated submissions and improve comment integrity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: CAPTCHA historically required human input; reCAPTCHA v3 uses risk-scoring without user interaction. These tools primarily deter bots and may incidentally reduce malattributed comments. Agencies should be aware of advances that may limit CAPTCHA effectiveness and choose appropriate versions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Verification of authorized mass-submitters via Regulations.gov API
rubrics_metrics.description: Allow authorized entities to post mass comment campaigns through an API after verification by GSA using a commercial identity validation service, while not verifying individual commenters.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This approach permits verified organizations to submit mass campaigns while still avoiding blanket verification of all individuals. It aims to 'assure such entities are who they say they are,' but does not solve abuse by unverified mass operators.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not categorically exclude computer-generated comments; assess relevance and authenticity
rubrics_metrics.description: Computer-generated comments may qualify as 'persons' under the APA's broad definitions; agencies should not automatically refuse to consider them but should assess their relevance, reliability, authenticity, and uniqueness of content.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts considering challenges may analogize to evidentiary standards (relevance, reliability, authenticity). Agencies should evaluate whether a computer-generated comment brings unique, material information not otherwise raised and document treatment; exclusionary practices risk failing to consider 'significant issues' required by the APA.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ensure automated screening does not exclude comments raising significant issues
rubrics_metrics.description: If authentication or screening technology filters comments, agencies must ensure the process does not automatically exclude submissions that raise unique, significant issues requiring consideration and response.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because agencies remain obligated to consider and respond to significant comments, any front-end filters should account for the obligation to preserve substantive inputs. Automated exclusion of comments that contain unique, relevant issues could undermine the agency's duty under the APA.

rubrics_metrics.name: Forensic indicators for identifying computer-generated or mass comments
rubrics_metrics.description: Use textual and meta-data indicators—repeated phrases/search-and-replace patterns, brevity, identical or near-identical submissions, large numbers posted at the same second, repeated email-address patterns/domains, uniformity in name/address/email formats, and low rates of confirmation requests—to detect probable automated or mass campaigns.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples from the FCC net neutrality docket: recurring sentence templates with substitutable tokens, millions of near-duplicates, spikes of 75,000+ comments in the same second, many comments tied to disposable email generators, and few requests for email confirmations. These signals are more useful for retrospective identification but can inform intake review and de-duplication.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use de-duplication tools to extract unique substantive content
rubrics_metrics.description: Employ de-duplication software to identify unique content within large volumes of duplicate or near-duplicate comments, treating the task as one of isolating unique issues for agency consideration.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Agencies commonly view computer-generated comments as a de-duplication challenge; de-duplication helps surface the unique substantive material that requires response. This reduces the resource burden of massive, repetitive dockets.

rubrics_metrics.name: Primary focus on substantive significant issues regardless of source
rubrics_metrics.description: Agencies should prioritize identifying and responding to significant issues raised in comments, regardless of whether the comment is human-authored, computer-generated, malattributed, or mass-submitted.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interviewed agency staff emphasized that 'the substance of comments... matters' more than identity or volume. Even when suspecting automation or malattribution, agencies should ensure obligations under the APA to consider and respond to significant substantive points are met; discovery of automated origin does not automatically negate substantive relevance.
